claims.text: High configurational entropy is an inherent feature of high-entropy alloys.
High configurational entropy lowers the effective activation energies for selective outward diffusion of oxide-forming elements such as Al and Cr.
Faster selective outward diffusion enables rapid nucleation and stabilization of a coherent, defect-controlled protective oxide layer.
The resulting protective oxide layer remains adherent under high-temperature oxidizing conditions.
The proposed initial material is a homogenized multi-principal-element HEA without a preformed oxide layer.
The controlled comparison exposes an HEA and a conventional lower-entropy alloy of similar overall chemistry to identical oxidation conditions between 800 and 1100 °C.
Selective diffusion pathways produce localized surface segregation of oxide-forming elements.
Localized surface segregation promotes formation of dense, coherent Al2O3 or Cr2O3 phases.
Diffusion kinetics govern phase formation and microstructural evolution.
DFT and kinetic Monte Carlo simulations predict that configurational entropy in HEAs broadens the distribution of diffusion activation energies.
A broadened distribution of diffusion activation energies facilitates selective, faster outward migration of protective oxide-forming elements.
Outward migration of oxide-forming elements promotes nucleation of a dense, defect-controlled oxide scale.
A dense, defect-controlled oxide scale limits oxygen ingress and thereby resists excessive growth and spallation.
Relative to the conventional-alloy baseline, the HEA will form a thinner, more uniform, more adherent, less porous oxide layer with fewer defects and a more consistent elemental distribution.
A lower-entropy conventional alloy develops its oxide less controllably, potentially producing greater porosity or a less uniform elemental distribution.
Temperature alters oxidation products and oxidation behavior in HEAs.
Oxygen partial pressure and oxide-forming-element concentration can alter the proposed diffusion and oxidation behavior.
Cross-sectional microstructural analysis and elemental mapping can be used to examine oxide evolution and elemental distributions in an oxidized HEA.

Failure of the HEA to exhibit both lower effective diffusion activation energies and a denser, more uniform, adherent protective oxide than the control would falsify the proposed entropy-driven mechanism.
